To determine how many of the three statements are true, we first identify the elements of set $S$. The problem defines $S$ as the set of integers $n$ satisfying $1 < n < 2$. Since there are no integers strictly between 1 and 2, $S$ is the empty set ($\emptyset$).

Now we evaluate each statement based on the properties of quantification over an empty set:
(i) "For all $n \in S$, $n$ is prime." This is a universal quantification $\forall n \in \emptyset, P(n)$. In mathematical logic, any universal quantification over an empty domain is vacuously true. Therefore, statement (i) is True.
(ii) "There exists $n \in S$ such that $n$ is prime." This is an existential quantification $\exists n \in \emptyset, P(n)$. An existential quantification over an empty set is always false because there are no elements in the set to satisfy the predicate. Therefore, statement (ii) is False.
(iii) "For all $n \in S$, $n$ is not prime." This is another universal quantification $\forall n \in \emptyset, Q(n)$, where $Q(n)$ is the property of not being prime. Like statement (i), this is vacuously true regardless of the predicate. Therefore, statement (iii) is True.

The statements that are true are (i) and (iii). The number of true statements is 2.

<ANSWER>2</ANSWER>
